lec05kp26-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp26-u01-p1-title.text: Every number here comes from one small experiment: 1000 + 20 training points, tested on 5100 new points

lec05kp26-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p1-bridge.text: The AdaBoost of KP25 degrades with noisy labels. Is a high accuracy reliable when one class has only 20 samples? First, how the experiment is made.

lec05kp26-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp26-setup
lec05kp26-u01-p1-fig1.text: Scatter of one training set: 1000 blue majority points centred at (0,0) and 20 orange rare points centred at (2,0), overlapping; below it the training, test, repeat count and RBF SVM parameters.

image.alt: Scatter of one training set: 1000 blue majority points centred at (0,0) and 20 orange rare points centred at (2,0), overlapping; below it the training, test, repeat count and RBF SVM parameters.

lec05kp26-u01-p1-term:類別不平衡.name: term:Class imbalance
lec05kp26-u01-p1-term:類別不平衡.text: **Class imbalance**: one class has very many samples and another very few; common in text classification, rare diseases, oil-spill detection.

lec05kp26-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p1-c1.text: **Data** (designed here, program-generated): majority $N((0,0),I)$, rare $N((2,0),I)$, independent coordinates, standard deviation 1; training 1000 + 20 points, one fixed test set of 5000 + 100.

lec05kp26-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp26-u01-p1-c2.text: **Model and repeats**: RBF-kernel SVM ($e^{-0.5\|x-z\|^2}$, $C=1$); one training set per random seed 0 to 19, 20 runs, averaged.

lec05kp26-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp26-u01-p2-title.text: Count the rare points caught and the false alarms and every measure follows: accuracy 98.0% vs 98.1%

lec05kp26-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p2-bridge.text: Every number comes from this experiment: 20 rare points among 1000 majority ones, tested on 5100 new points where the rare class is only 2%. How is a classifier scored?

lec05kp26-u01-p2-term:召回率.name: term:Recall
lec05kp26-u01-p2-term:召回率.text: **Recall**: share of the 100 rare points caught, $=\text{TP}/100$; **precision**: share of points called rare that are, $=\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FP})$. TP: rare points caught; FP: false alarms.

lec05kp26-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p2-c1.text: **Accuracy** $=(\text{TP}+\text{TN})/5100$, $\text{TN}=5000-\text{FP}$. **Always the majority**: TP 0, FP 0, recall $0/100=0$, accuracy $5000/5100=98.0\%$.

lec05kp26-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp26-u01-p3-title.text: The simpler the classifier, the less it cares about 20 points: SVM C from 0.01 to 100 catches 0 to 16.85

lec05kp26-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p3-bridge.text: The SVM catches only 5.85 rare points on average and treats the other 94 as majority. Why does a classifier ignore the rare class?

lec05kp26-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p3-c1.text: **Reasoning** (source): for generalization we ask for simple classifiers (regularization, pruning); a simple hypothesis ignores rare cases, and ignoring 20 points barely changes the total cost.

lec05kp26-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp26-u01-p3-c2.text: **SVM**: $C$ penalizes a misclassified point (KP15). $C=0.01$, $0.1$: TP 0, FP 0; $C=1$: TP 5.85; $C=100$: TP 16.85, FP 10.9. Recall $=\text{TP}/100$; accuracy about 98%.

lec05kp26-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp26-u01-p4-title.text: Imbalance alone is no disease: at 1000 to 100 an easy task keeps 91.6% recall, a hard one 14.9%

lec05kp26-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p4-bridge.text: The simpler the classifier, the less it cares about 20 points. Is it always bad whenever the classes are imbalanced?

lec05kp26-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p4-c1.text: **Source** (Japkowicz): a large imbalance need not hurt; read it with task difficulty and training size. An easy task or much data may be fine; a hard task or too few points makes even a small imbalance fatal.

lec05kp26-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp26-u01-p4-c2.text: **How** (designed here): RBF SVM ($C=1$, $\gamma=0.5$); training majority:rare $=100{:}100$, $1000{:}100$, $1000{:}10$, $10000{:}100$, $10000{:}10$; fixed test 2000 + 2000, recall $=\text{TP}/2000$; centres 4 (easy) or 1.5 (hard) apart.

lec05kp26-u01-p4-c3.name: u01-p4-c3
lec05kp26-u01-p4-c3.text: **Results**: easy-task recall 97.5, 91.6, 66.8, 78.1, 43.2%; hard task 78.6, 14.9, 0, 0, 0%. With 10 rare points even the easy task does poorly.

lec05kp26-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp26-u01-p5-title.text: Data cures: oversampling catches 68.15, undersampling 77.05, false alarms rise from 2 to 606 and 757

lec05kp26-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p5-bridge.text: Imbalance is not always bad, but on a hard task 1000 to 100 presses the recall to 14.9%. The first cure changes the data: copy the rare class or drop majority points, with what result?

lec05kp26-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p5-c1.text: **Method**: oversampling draws 980 more from the 20 rare points with replacement, so training becomes 1000 + 1000; undersampling keeps 20 of the 1000 majority points at random without replacement, so training becomes 20 + 20. The same SVM ($C=1$).

lec05kp26-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp26-u01-p5-c2.text: **Results** (TP / FP): plain 5.85 / 2; oversampling 68.15 / 605.55; undersampling 77.05 / 756.7. Example: oversampling recall $68.15/100=68.2\%$, precision $68.15/(68.15+605.55)=10.1\%$.

lec05kp26-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp26-u01-p5-c3.text: **Price**: the rare class is found, but precision drops to about 10% and accuracy to 85% to 88%.

lec05kp26-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp26-u01-p6-title.text: Focused undersampling: how many to keep is hard; 20 kept catch 82.7 with 2126 false alarms, 60 catch 11.45

lec05kp26-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p6-bridge.text: Oversampling and undersampling were random, with many false alarms. Would it be better to drop only the majority points far from the boundary, which carry no information?

lec05kp26-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p6-c1.text: **Method**: delete points far from the boundary (source). Steps: a first SVM ($C=1$) scores the 1000 majority points; keep the $m$ with the largest scores (most like the rare class), retrain on 20 rare + $m$; $m=20,60,100,200$.

lec05kp26-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp26-u01-p6-c3.text: **Meaning**: the right target distribution is open (source): 20 vs 60 kept differ hugely; 2126 false alarms at 20 kept, 757 for random undersampling.

lec05kp26-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp26-u01-p7-title.text: Cost-sensitive: leave the data alone; a 50 times rare-class C catches 70.2, AdaBoost weight 50 catches 61.9

lec05kp26-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p7-bridge.text: Focused undersampling: how many to keep is hard, and 20 kept gave 2126 false alarms. What does the cost-sensitive cure, changing the classifier and not the data, achieve?

lec05kp26-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p7-c1.text: **Method** (source): weight the rare class more. SVM: rare-class $C$ 50 times larger (weights 25.5 vs 0.51); AdaBoost: 100 stumps, rare initial weight $\times w$, $w=1,10,50$, then normalized.

lec05kp26-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp26-u01-p8-title.text: To remember: harm = simplicity preference × rare class; change the data or the cost

lec05kp26-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p8-bridge.text: Changing the cost, like changing the data, raised TP and FP together and cut precision. What should be remembered, and how should one evaluate?

lec05kp26-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p8-c1.text: **To remember** (source): the harm does not come from the numbers being different but from the interaction of the simplicity preference with the rare class. Two cures: change the data (resampling) or change the cost (weighting).

lec05kp26-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp26-u01-p8-c2.text: **Evaluation**: look at recall and precision, not only accuracy; always saying the majority also scores 98.0%.

lec05kp26-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp26-u01-p8-c3.text: **Reminder** (source): class imbalance matters a great deal in practice; a designer must be aware of it and alert to the cures.

lec05kp26-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp26-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: the cures raise points caught and false alarms together; balanced accuracy 0.53 to about 0.8

lec05kp26-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p9-bridge.text: What to remember is the trade-off. With the four treatments in one table and a measure that sees the rare class, does any clearly win?

lec05kp26-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp26-u01-p9-c1.text: **Balanced accuracy** $=(\text{recall}+\text{specificity})/2$, specificity $=\text{TN}/5000$; always the majority $(0+1)/2=0.50$. Example: plain SVM $(0.0585+4998/5000)/2=0.53$.

lec05kp26-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp26-u01-p9-c2.text: **SVM** (TP / FP / balanced accuracy): plain 5.85 / 2 / 0.53; oversampling 68.15 / 605.55 / 0.78; undersampling 77.05 / 756.7 / 0.81; cost-sensitive 70.2 / 619.3 / 0.79.

lec05kp26-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp26-u01-p9-c3.text: **Tree** (min leaf 5): plain 21 / 29.85 / 0.60; oversampling 33.75 / 101.45 / 0.66; undersampling 77.85 / 912.6 / 0.80; cost-sensitive 43.15 / 227.7 / 0.69. None clearly wins.

lec05kp26-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp26-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, accuracy, recall and balanced accuracy of two classifiers

lec05kp26-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p10-bridge.text: Balanced accuracy leaves always saying the majority at 0.50. Back to the definitions: compute by hand the measures of A, which says majority for everyone, and of B, which catches 6: what are they?

lec05kp26-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp26-u01-p10-q1.text: **Setup**: 1000 negatives and 10 positives (the rare class). A says negative for everyone; B catches 6 of the 10 positives and raises 40 false alarms.

lec05kp26-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp26-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 1**: what are the accuracy and recall of A and B?

lec05kp26-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp26-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: what are the balanced accuracies of A and B?

lec05kp26-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp26-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2, A has the higher accuracy and is useless

lec05kp26-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for the accuracy, recall and balanced accuracy of A and B. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp26-u01-p11-a1.name: u01-p11-a1
lec05kp26-u01-p11-a1.text: **Question 1**: A: TP 0, FN 10, FP 0, TN 1000; accuracy $1000/1010=0.990$, recall 0. B: TP 6, FN 4, FP 40, TN 960; accuracy $966/1010=0.956$, recall 0.6.

lec05kp26-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp26-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: A has the higher accuracy yet catches no rare point; B has a precision of only $6/46=0.13$, which is the trade-off.

steps.label: Class imbalance
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C19. The facts that class imbalance harms classifiers, that the harm comes from the interaction of the simplicity preference with the rare class, that imbalance must be read together with task difficulty and data size, the two families of cures, focused resampling, the open problem of the target distribution and the 'to remember' line follow the source. All experiments were designed for this lecture (added): page 1 gives the data, model and parameters, page 2 computes recall, precision and accuracy from the raw counts (TP, FP), and every later table lists the counts. Numbers were recomputed by a program as means of 20 runs, and the pages state honestly that always saying the majority scores about the same accuracy as a standard SVM, that the cures raise the points caught but also the false alarms, that focused undersampling is very sensitive to how many points are kept and that a rare class of only 10 points hurts even an easy task. The notes are published with the file and contain no student ID, grade or exam item.

steps.label: How the experiment works
steps.speakerNotes: The AdaBoost of KP25 degrades with noisy labels. This page asks whether even a high accuracy is reliable when one class has only 20 samples. Before answering, the experiment behind every number of this lesson is spelled out. Class imbalance means one class has very many samples and another very few, common in text classification, rare diseases and oil-spill detection in satellite images. The data were generated by a program: the majority class comes from a 2-D Gaussian centred at the origin and the rare class from one centred at (2,0), coordinates independent with standard deviation 1, so the centres are 2 apart and the clouds overlap a lot. The training set is 1000 majority points plus 20 rare points, blue for the majority and orange for the rare class in the figure; the test set is one fixed set of 5000 majority points plus 100 rare points, and every method is tested on the same one. The model is an SVM with the RBF kernel, e to the minus 0.5 times the squared distance, with C equal to 1. The training set is drawn once for each random seed 0 to 19, so every number is a mean of 20 runs. The next page asks how to score a classifier on the 5100 test points.

steps.label: From counts to measures
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page buried 20 rare points among 1000 majority points. This page asks how to score a classifier on the 5100 test points. Two new words first. Recall is the share of the 100 rare points that are caught, TP divided by 100, where TP is the number of rare points caught. Precision is the share of points called rare that really are rare, TP divided by TP plus FP, where FP is the number of false alarms, majority points called rare. Accuracy is the share of all points called right: TP plus 5000 minus FP, divided by 5100. First always the majority: TP is 0 and FP is 0, recall 0 over 100 is 0 and accuracy 5000 over 5100 is 98.0%. Now the SVM, whose counts averaged over 20 runs are TP 5.85 and FP 2: recall 5.85 over 100 is 5.9%, precision 5.85 over 7.85 is 74.5% and accuracy, 5.85 plus 4998 over 5100, is 98.1%. Precision is always the mean counts divided, so every number in a table can be checked by hand. A common question: 98.0% and 98.1% are so close, did the SVM learn anything? The next page asks why a classifier ignores the rare class.

steps.label: The simplicity preference
steps.speakerNotes: On the previous page the SVM caught only 5.85 rare points on average. This page asks why a classifier ignores the rare class. The reasoning, as the source says: for generalization we keep asking for simple classifiers, with regularization and pruning; a simple hypothesis does not bother with rare cases, and ignoring 20 points barely changes the total cost. The experiment was designed here, with the same data as the previous page. The C of the SVM is the penalty for one misclassified point and a larger C means less regularization: with C of 0.01 and 0.1 both TP and FP are 0, which is always the majority; C of 1 gives TP 5.85; C of 100 gives TP 16.85 and FP 10.9, so recall, TP over 100, is about 16.9%; accuracy stays about 98%. The decision tree is CART with at least k training points per leaf, a larger k being simpler: k of 1 gives TP 23.25 and FP 73.1; k of 5 gives 21 and 29.85; k of 20 gives 9.45 and 12.55; k of 50 gives all zeros. The pattern: the simpler, the fewer caught. The next page asks whether imbalance is always harmful.

steps.label: Difficulty and data size
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the simpler the classifier, the less it cares about 20 points. This page asks whether it is always bad whenever the classes are imbalanced. The source is Japkowicz's study: a large imbalance need not hurt; read it with task difficulty and the number of training points. The experiment was designed here: the same RBF SVM with C equal to 1 and gamma equal to 0.5, with training sets of majority to rare of 100 to 100, 1000 to 100, 1000 to 10, 10000 to 100 and 10000 to 10; this time the test set is fixed at 2000 majority and 2000 rare points, so recall is TP over 2000. The easy task has the two centres 4 apart and the hard task 1.5 apart, standard deviation 1 in both. Easy-task recall is 97.5%, 91.6%, 66.8%, 78.1% and 43.2% in order; the hard task gives 78.6% and 14.9%, the other three about 0. The small print under each cell of the table is TP, which can be divided by 2000 to check. Conclusion: with only 10 rare points even the easy task does poorly, and the ratio is not the only factor. The next page looks at the first cure.

steps.label: Changing the data
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that on a hard task 1000 to 100 presses recall to 14.9%. This page asks what the first cure, changing the data by copying the rare class or dropping majority points, achieves. Method: oversampling draws 980 more from the 20 rare points with replacement, so training becomes 1000 plus 1000; undersampling keeps 20 of the 1000 majority points at random without replacement, so training becomes 20 plus 20. Both use the same SVM with C equal to 1 and the same 5000 plus 100 test set as page 1. The TP and FP: plain 5.85 and 2; oversampling 68.15 and 605.55; undersampling 77.05 and 756.7. Worked example: oversampling recall is 68.15 over 100, 68.2%, and precision is 68.15 over 68.15 plus 605.55, 10.1%. The pattern: TP rises but FP rises much more, so precision falls to about 10% and accuracy to 85% to 88%. The next page asks whether dropping only the majority points far from the boundary does better.

steps.label: Focused resampling
steps.speakerNotes: On the previous page random resampling gave many false alarms. This page asks whether dropping only the majority points far from the boundary, which carry no information, would do better. Focused undersampling deletes the points far from the boundary, which is the source's idea. My concrete steps: train a first SVM on the 20 plus 1000 points with C equal to 1, compute its decision value for each of the 1000 majority points, the largest values being the points most like the rare class and nearest the boundary; keep the m largest, then retrain on the 20 rare points plus those m, with m of 20, 60, 100 and 200. TP, FP and accuracy: 20 kept gives 82.7, 2126.05 and 58.0%; 60 gives 11.45, 55.5 and 97.2%; 100 gives 8.3, 32.55 and 97.6%; 200 gives 5.95, 2 and 98.1%; keeping all 1000 returns to the plain SVM. Meaning: the right target distribution is an open problem, 20 and 60 kept differ hugely, and with 20 kept the false alarms are 2126, more than the 757 of random undersampling. The next page asks what the cost-sensitive cure, changing the classifier and not the data, achieves.

steps.label: Changing the cost
steps.speakerNotes: On the previous page focused undersampling had to decide how many points to keep, which is hard. This page asks what the cost-sensitive cure, changing the classifier and not the data, achieves. Method, as the source says: give the rare class a heavier weight. For the SVM the rare-class C is set to 50 times the majority one, the actual class weights being 25.5 against 0.51, a ratio of exactly 50; AdaBoost uses 100 decision stumps and multiplies the rare initial weight by w, with w of 1, 10 and 50, then normalizes, the weights of KP25 having been made for hard samples anyway. SVM result: TP 70.2 and FP 619.3, recall 70.2% and precision 70.2 over 70.2 plus 619.3, 10.2%. AdaBoost: w of 1 gives TP 20.1 and FP 16.65; w of 10 gives 48.3 and 160.65; w of 50 gives 61.9 and 373.75; recall 20.1%, 48.3% and 61.9%, precision 54.7%, 23.1% and 14.2%. The pattern: the heavier the rare class, the more TP and FP rise together and the more precision falls, the same trade-off as changing the data. The next page asks what should be remembered.

steps.label: To remember
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said recall rose and precision fell under all cures. This page asks what should be remembered and how to evaluate. To remember, as the source says: the harm does not come from the numbers being different but from the interaction of the simplicity preference with the rare class; two cures: change the data, by resampling, or change the cost, by weighting. Evaluation: look at recall and precision, not only accuracy; always saying the majority also scores 98.0%. Reminder from the source: class imbalance matters a great deal in practice; a designer must be aware of it and alert to the cures. The next extension page looks at balanced accuracy.

steps.label: Extension: comparing the cures and balanced accuracy
steps.speakerNotes: The conclusion of the previous page was the trade-off. This page asks whether any of four treatments clearly wins when they are put in one table with a measure that sees the rare class. Balanced accuracy is the mean of recall and specificity, specificity being TN over 5000, the share of majority points called right; always the majority gives 0 plus 1 over 2, which is 0.50. Worked example: the plain SVM has recall 0.0585 and specificity 4998 over 5000, 0.9996, a mean of 0.53. TP, FP and balanced accuracy of the four SVM treatments: plain 5.85, 2 and 0.53; oversampling 68.15, 605.55 and 0.78; undersampling 77.05, 756.7 and 0.81; cost-sensitive 70.2, 619.3 and 0.79. Decision tree with at least 5 points per leaf: plain 21, 29.85 and 0.60; oversampling 33.75, 101.45 and 0.66; undersampling 77.85, 912.6 and 0.80; cost-sensitive 43.15, 227.7 and 0.69. None clearly wins; the difference is a trade-off between how many rare points to catch and how many false alarms to accept. The next page practises balanced accuracy by hand.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said balanced accuracy leaves always saying the majority at 0.50. This page poses an exercise back on the definitions: 1000 negatives and 10 positives, the positives being the rare class. A says negative for everyone; B catches 6 of the 10 positives and raises 40 false alarms. Question 1: what are the accuracy and recall of A and B? Question 2: what are the balanced accuracies of A and B? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: A: TP 0, FN 10, FP 0, TN 1000; accuracy 1000 over 1010, which is 0.990, and recall 0. B: TP 6, FN 4, FP 40, TN 960; accuracy 966 over 1010, which is 0.956, and recall 0.6. Question 2: A: 0 plus 1 over 2, which is 0.5. B: specificity 960 over 1000, which is 0.96, and 0.6 plus 0.96 over 2, which is 0.78. Check: A has the higher accuracy yet catches no rare point; B has a precision of only 6 over 46, which is 0.13, and that is the trade-off. That finishes the 26 knowledge points of the chapter.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP26: the class imbalance problem (undergraduate, self-study)
